Chapter 51

The exit criteria: what a DPE 8++ in Svelte can do

What “8++” means for this course, measured: every surface the coverage plan assigned to a chapter, with what you should be able to do with it and where it was taught — or declined, deferred or dropped, and why. Twelve production exercises that start where the course stops, a rubric, and the routine that keeps you current.

By the end of this chapter

Measure yourself against every Svelte and SvelteKit surface the course planned, honestly — and pick the exercises that close the gaps you find.

“8++” is a promise about coverage and about reasons. Every surface the coverage plan named for Svelte 5.57 and SvelteKit 3.0.1 — 561 of them — is in one of four states in this course: used for something in Meridian, with the reason written down; declined, with the reason written down; on the backlog, with the reason it waits; or dropped, with the reason it was not built. The plan is this course’s own list and not the whole API, so a built-in nobody planned has no row here. The 3.1.0 minor the project now runs on brought two such cases — the CSP hash-reporting keywords and the sveltekit.endpoint span arrived after the plan was drawn — and chapters 47 and 37 say where they apply. Nothing is demonstrated for its own sake, and nothing is claimed that the code does not do. This chapter is the list, and it is the hardest chapter in the course to fake, because it is not written by hand.

Why this list can be trusted

It was generated from the two documents that decided the course — the coverage plan, which assigned each surface to a chapter, and the gap list, which recorded what was then built, deferred or dropped — by tools/exit-criteria.js, and committed as content/surfaces.json. Then verify.js holds it to the course on every build: a surface marked taught must be in backticks in the prose of the chapter it names, a deferred one must sit under an item of the backlog in chapter 50 — and, when the row says that item names it, the item’s own text must carry it in backticks — and every planned chapter must have a row. Mark one deferred surface taught and the build fails. Today the list has 561 surfaces: 366 taught, 11 declined, 176 deferred and 8 dropped.

Read each table with one question per row: can I do what the middle column says, without this course open? “Use it, and say why Meridian does” means both halves — the code and the reason. “Read it in older code, and say what replaced it” is the migration chapter’s history. “Say what it would take” is the backlog: knowing what you have not built, and why it waits, is part of the skill. Where a row says the *planned use* is on the backlog, the plan imagined a use of the surface that nobody has built, and the surface may or may not be in the code; where it says what is installed and what waits, as for tracing.current, it is in the code in part. The groups follow the order of Svelte’s own documentation index.

Twelve production exercises

The checklist measures what you know. These measure what you can ship. Each starts where the course stops, names the chapters it draws on, and says what “done” looks like; several build an item from the backlog, which is the point — the backlog is real work with the reasoning already done.

  1. Add a fourth, right-to-left locale (chapters 21, 23, 36). A Paraglide messages file, %paraglide.dir%, an audit of every physical CSS property, the guides prerendered in the new language, and the sitemap from the backlog with an alternate per locale. Done: the guides ship in four languages, and a right-to-left page has no physical margin anywhere.
  2. Give a trip a cover image, then move it to object storage (chapters 33, 48, 47). First the upload: fields.cover.as('file'), v.file(), sharp, BODY_SIZE_LIMIT. Then a signed upload from a command, the bucket in connect-src, handleFetch for the server’s side. Done: an image that never passes through the app server.
  3. Rate-limit sign-in, then share the limit across two containers (chapters 47, 48, 19). A token bucket on getClientAddress(), then a shared store — and the live rooms need the same pub/sub. Done: the eleventh sign-in from one address is a 429 on either container.
  4. Export the traces to an OTLP collector, and keep /diagnostics working (chapters 37, 48). A second exporter and the bundling caveats. Done: the same span in the collector and on the page.
  5. Write an sv add-on for this series (chapters 03, 49) that writes src/env.ts, the href() helper and the three-handler hooks.server.ts: defineAddon, sv/testing, published with the sv-add keyword. Done: npx sv add on a fresh scaffold writes files this course could quote.
  6. Run a dependency that ships Svelte 4 components inside Meridian (chapters 49, 45). Legacy mode, compatibility.componentApi, the codes it raises, and the migration script on a fork. Done: it renders, and you can name every warning it printed.
  7. Ship the waypoint docs site to GitHub Pages and to one platform adapter (chapters 09, 48). @sveltejs/adapter-static, paths.base, a fallback page; then platform and emulate. Done: both serve the same pages, and you can say what broke on the second.
  8. Make the itinerary writable offline (chapters 39, 32, 19). A command queue in IndexedDB, replayed on online, with a conflict policy against the live query’s last-writer-wins. Done: a stop added in a tunnel reaches a companion when the train comes out, and a conflict is reported, not lost.
  9. Tighten the CSP to style-src 'self' (chapters 47, 37). Turn on csp.reportOnly with the stricter policy and an endpoint for the reports, count the violations, move the inline styles, then enforce. Done: no 'unsafe-inline', and a quiet report endpoint.
  10. Require Trusted Types (chapters 47, 45). require-trusted-types-for 'script', policies for MapLibre, three.js and Tiptap, and Svelte’s fragments: 'tree'. Done: the browser enforces it and every screen still works.
  11. Run the whole sv migrate routine on a SvelteKit 2 project of your own, and ship it (chapters 49, 03). One commit per task, MIGRATION_TASKS.md resolved with evidence, the @migration-task grep clean. Done: your record reads like docs/migration-sveltekit-3.md.
  12. Build the invite-email outbox (chapters 20, 21, 41). render() for the body, a table written in the same transaction as the invite, a worker that drains it, the mail in the inviter’s language. Done: an invite sent while the mail server is down arrives when it comes back.

Scoring

  • Knowledge — for every declined and dropped row, you can explain the trade without looking it up: what the surface would have bought, and why Meridian does without it.
  • Practice — you have shipped the “done” of at least three exercises, in a branch with tests that failed before and pass after.
  • Depth — you can read the adapter you deploy (chapter 48) and the compiler’s messages (chapter 45) without the documentation open.
  • Currency — you can say what the next minor of Svelte or SvelteKit would change in Meridian, because you ran the routine: get-documentation for the release notes, sv migrate on a branch, verify (chapter 50).

Checkpoint

  • You can map any surface in the Svelte or SvelteKit documentation to a file in Meridian, or to the sentence that declines it.
  • You have done at least three of the twelve exercises.
  • You can run the upgrade routine and the migration routine without this course open.
